question: How do you structure OTE for a 6-person SDR team in 2027?
body:
## Direct Answer Structure OTE (on-target earnings) for a 6-person SDR team in 2027 as a base-plus-variable package where the base covers roughly 60–70% of total pay and the variable 30–40% is tied to meetings booked and pipeline that survives qualification — not raw activity. Anchor the mix to your sales cycle and average deal size, keep quota attainment reachable for the middle of the team (60–70% hitting target), and make ramping reps a distinct pay tier so you don't burn cash on people who can't yet produce. The whole plan should be simple enough that any SDR can calculate their own paycheck in under a minute. The hard part of SDR compensation is not picking a number — it's picking the *right ratio and the right metric* so the plan pulls reps toward the behavior that actually feeds your account executives. A 6-person team is a specific size: big enough that you can't manage by vibes and small enough that one bad plan quietly bleeds the whole top of funnel. This guide walks through the base/variable split, what to pay on, how to handle ramp and accelerators, and how to pressure-test the whole thing before you sign off on it for 2027. ## What base-to-variable split should an SDR OTE use in 2027? The default that has held up across most B2B SaaS orgs is a **60/40 to 70/30 base-to-variable split** for SDRs, and 2027 hasn't changed the physics behind it. SDRs sit at the top of the funnel where outcomes are noisier and less within their direct control than a closing rep's — a meeting can be booked perfectly and still get disqualified for reasons the SDR never touched. When the person controls less of the final outcome, you weight their pay toward base to keep them stable, focused, and retained. Pushing SDRs to a 50/50 split (the classic AE ratio) tends to backfire: it introduces income volatility onto a role that's already high-churn, and it rewards the wrong risk tolerance for a job that's fundamentally about consistent daily volume. For a concrete frame, imagine a mid-market SaaS team setting SDR OTE somewhere in the common US range for the role. If you land on a 65/35 split, roughly two-thirds of every rep's earnings arrive predictably every pay period and one-third rides on performance. That predictability is a feature, not a weakness. The variable portion still needs to be *large enough to matter* — if the at-risk pay is under about 25% of total, most reps mentally treat it as a bonus rather than a driver and it stops steering behavior. Below is the decision logic most RevOps leaders walk when they set the ratio, and you can read more on the mechanics of splitting pay in our [comp-plan fundamentals guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-comp-split-basics). ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Setting SDR base/variable split] --> B{How much of the outcome
does the SDR control?} B -->|Low control:
long cycle, heavy AE
disqualification| C[70/30 split
weight toward base] B -->|Medium control:
clean qualification,
fast handoff| D[65/35 split
balanced default] B -->|High control:
SDR owns qualification
+ some conversion| E[60/40 split
more upside] C --> F{Is variable still
>= 25% of OTE?} D --> F E --> F F -->|No| G[Raise variable weight —
bonus is too small to
drive behavior] F -->|Yes| H[Split is viable —
move to metric design] ``` One more nuance for 2027 specifically: with more teams running blended human-plus-AI prospecting (AI drafting sequences, enriching lists, scoring intent), the SDR's job is shifting toward the *judgment* parts — which accounts to prioritize, how to personalize an opener, when to break from the sequence. That shift slightly *strengthens* the case for a healthy base, because you're paying increasingly for skill and discernment rather than dial-count. Don't let the AI-productivity narrative talk you into a thinner base; pay for the higher-value work you now expect. ## What metric should the variable pay be tied to? This is where most SDR comp plans quietly break. The temptation is to pay on **activity** — dials, emails, connects — because it's easy to measure and always moving. Don't. Activity metrics reward motion, not outcomes, and they invite gaming: a rep will happily book garbage meetings that no-show or instantly disqualify to hit a "meetings set" number. The metric you pay on becomes the metric you get more of, exactly as specified, including all the loopholes. The strongest primary metric for SDR variable pay in 2027 is a **qualified, held meeting** — usually defined as a meeting that the AE accepts *and* that actually occurs (the prospect shows up) *and* that clears an agreed qualification bar (SQL/SQO or your equivalent). Some teams go one layer deeper and pay a smaller kicker on **pipeline that survives to a later stage** or on sourced closed-won, which ties the SDR to real revenue and discourages sandbagging weak opportunities into the funnel. The trade-off is attribution lag: paying on closed-won means the SDR waits a full sales cycle to see money, which hurts motivation on the daily grind. A practical compromise is a two-part variable: the bulk paid on the qualified-held meeting (fast, motivating, weekly-visible) and a smaller accelerator paid on opportunities that convert. See our [breakdown of activity-vs-outcome metrics](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-sdr-metrics) for the fuller argument. Whatever you choose, write the **definition down and make both the SDR and the AE sign it.** The single largest source of SDR comp disputes is a fuzzy line between "meeting booked" and "meeting that counts." Specify: What makes a meeting qualified? Who adjudicates a disputed disqualification? What happens to pay if the AE reschedules and the prospect ghosts? A one-page rules-of-engagement document prevents 90% of the end-of-month arguments, and it protects the reps as much as it protects you — an SDR should never lose earned credit because an AE was sloppy on the handoff. ## How do you set a fair, reachable quota for the team? Quota is where the OTE becomes real, because OTE is by definition the pay *at 100% of quota*. If your quota is set so high that only your top rep ever reaches it, then "OTE" is a fiction and everyone else is effectively underpaid relative to the number you advertised when recruiting — which is how you build a resentful, high-attrition team. The design target most compensation professionals use is that **60–70% of the team should be able to reach quota** in a normal period, with your best performers pushing well past it into accelerator territory and your bottom rung falling short in a way that signals a real performance conversation. To back into a defensible quota for a 6-person team, work bottom-up from capacity, not top-down from the revenue you wish you had. Estimate the realistic number of qualified-held meetings one fully-ramped SDR can generate per month given your motion, list quality, and tooling. Discount it for the reality of ramp, PTO, bad weeks, and disqualification rates. That per-rep number times your six seats (weighted for who's ramped versus ramping) is your *team* capacity — and if the pipeline target the business is handing you exceeds that capacity, the answer is not a punishing quota, it's more headcount or better tooling. Setting a quota above capacity doesn't create pipeline; it creates turnover and a spike in low-quality meetings as reps scramble to hit an impossible bar. The diagram below shows the sequence. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[1. Per-rep capacity:
realistic qualified
meetings/month] --> B[2. Discount for ramp,
PTO, disqualification,
bad weeks] B --> C[3. Multiply across
6 seats, weighted by
ramp status] C --> D[4. Team capacity] D --> E{Business pipeline
target <= team
capacity?} E -->|Yes| F[Set individual quota
so 60-70% can hit it] E -->|No| G[Add headcount or

inflate quota] F --> H[Validate: model
payout at 40/70/
100/130% attainment] ``` Once you have a quota, always **model the payout curve at several attainment levels before you approve the plan** — 40%, 70%, 100%, and 130% of quota. Look at what a rep earns at each. If someone at 70% attainment (a decent-not-great performer) is taking home barely above their base, the variable is too back-loaded and you'll lose the middle of your team. If someone at 130% is earning a fortune with no cap in sight, make sure your unit economics survive that outcome — you *want* to pay for overperformance, but you want to have chosen to. ## How should ramp and accelerators be handled? A new SDR is not a productive SDR, and paying them as if they were is a fast way to torch your comp budget. Build an explicit **ramp period** — commonly the first two to four months, matched to how long your onboarding and territory-learning actually take — during which the rep earns their full base but is on a **ramped quota or a guaranteed variable draw**. A ramped quota means their target scales up over the period (e.g., a fraction of full quota in month one, growing to full by the end of ramp). A guaranteed draw means you pay out the variable at a set level regardless of attainment while they learn, which protects the rep's income and your ability to recruit. Either works; the mistake is having no ramp policy at all and either overpaying beginners or scaring off good candidates with a cliff they can't clear in week one. For a 6-person team, define this once and apply it uniformly so every new hire is treated the same — inconsistency here reads as favoritism and poisons trust. On the top end, **accelerators** reward reps who blow past quota by paying a higher rate per meeting or per point of attainment above 100%. This is deliberate: overperformance is disproportionately valuable, and a rep who consistently produces 130% deserves to feel that in their paycheck, or they'll leave for a team that pays it. A common structure pays the standard rate up to 100% of quota and a multiplied rate (say, 1.25x–1.5x the base commission rate) on everything above. Decide consciously whether to **cap** payouts. The RevOps-standard view is *don't cap SDR earnings* — a cap tells your best rep to stop working once they've maxed out, which is exactly backward. If your finance team insists on a ceiling for budget predictability, set it high enough that only genuinely exceptional performance reaches it, and revisit it every year. Our [ramp and accelerator playbook](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-ramp-accelerators) has worked examples for both. The complementary question is **decelerators or a floor** — what happens to a rep who chronically underperforms. Comp shouldn't be the primary tool for managing a struggling SDR (that's a coaching and performance-management conversation), but the plan should make sustained underperformance visible and financially real without being so punishing that one bad month spirals a decent rep out the door. A common approach is a threshold below which variable pay is zero or minimal, set low enough that it only catches genuine non-performance, not a normal slow patch. ## How do you pay a 6-person team fairly — individual vs. team components? Six is a size where you have a real choice between **pure individual comp** and a **blended individual-plus-team model**, and the right answer depends on how your reps actually work. Pure individual pay — everyone earns only on their own qualified meetings — maximizes personal accountability and is the cleanest to administer. It's the default for good reason. But it can create a "lone wolf" culture where reps hoard the best accounts, refuse to share what's working, and treat teammates as competition rather than colleagues. A **small team component** — say, 10–20% of the variable tied to the team collectively hitting its number — can counterbalance that by giving everyone a stake in the group's success, which encourages senior SDRs to help ramping ones and reps to share winning sequences. The risk is free-riding: on a 6-person team one coaster can drag on five workers, and the workers notice. The pragmatic middle ground most 6-person teams land on is **mostly individual with a modest team kicker**, or purely individual comp paired with *non-monetary* team incentives (contests, spiffs, recognition) that build collaboration without diluting personal accountability. Keep the individual portion clearly dominant; the team piece should nudge culture, not determine anyone's rent. Whatever you build, **audit for internal fairness across the six seats.** Are territories or lead-flow roughly balanced, or does one rep sit on a gold mine while another works scraps? Unequal opportunity under an equal quota is the fastest way to lose your fair-minded people. If territories are genuinely unequal, either rebalance them or set per-rep quotas that reflect the real potential of each patch — never advertise a single OTE while quietly handing out unwinnable territories. Fairness in a small team is highly visible; everyone knows everyone's roughly-how-they're-doing, and a plan that's transparently equitable is worth more in retention than a few extra points of variable. ## Sources - [The Bridge Group — SDR Metrics & Compensation Report](https://bridgegroupinc.com/) - [RevOps Co-op — Sales Compensation Resources](https://www.revopscoop.com/) - [Sales Hacker — SDR Compensation Guides](https://www.saleshacker.com/) - [QuotaPath — Sales Commission & OTE Resources](https://www.quotapath.com/) - [Xactly — Incentive Compensation Research](https://www.xactlycorp.com/) - [CaptivateIQ — Commission Plan Design Library](https://www.captivateiq.com/) - [Gartner — Sales Compensation & B2B Sales Research](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales) - [Harvard Business Review — Motivating Salespeople](https://hbr.org/2015/04/motivating-salespeople-what-really-works) ## Related questions ### What is a typical SDR OTE range in 2027? It varies widely by region, industry, and market segment, so anchor to current local benchmark data (Bridge Group, Glassdoor, Pave) rather than a fixed figure. Structure the split — 60/40 to 70/30 base-to-variable — before you fixate on the total number. ### Should SDRs be paid on meetings booked or pipeline created? Pay primarily on qualified, held meetings for fast, motivating feedback, and add a smaller accelerator on pipeline that converts. Pure closed-won pay introduces too much attribution lag for a daily-volume role. ### How long should the SDR ramp period be? Typically two to four months, matched to your actual onboarding and territory-learning time. Pay full base with a ramped quota or a guaranteed variable draw so new hires aren't penalized for still learning. ### Should you cap SDR commissions? Generally no — caps tell your best performers to stop working once maxed out. If finance requires a ceiling for predictability, set it high enough that only exceptional performance reaches it and review it annually. ### What quota attainment rate signals a healthy plan? Aim for 60–70% of the team reaching quota in a normal period, top performers pushing into accelerators, and only the bottom rung falling short. If almost no one hits target, the quota is above capacity. ## FAQ **What does OTE actually mean for an SDR?** OTE (on-target earnings) is total annual pay a rep earns at exactly 100% of quota — base salary plus the variable/commission portion. It is a target, not a guarantee: reps below quota earn less and reps above it earn more, which is why the quota must be genuinely reachable for OTE to be an honest number. **Why not just pay SDRs a 50/50 split like AEs?** Because SDRs control less of the final outcome — a well-booked meeting can still be disqualified for reasons outside the SDR's hands. Weighting pay toward a 60–70% base keeps a high-churn, high-volume role stable and reduces income volatility, while still leaving 30–40% at-risk to drive performance. **How do I keep reps from booking junk meetings to hit their number?** Pay on *qualified, held* meetings rather than meetings merely booked, define "qualified" in a signed one-page rules-of-engagement document, and consider a small accelerator on opportunities that convert to later stages. Paying only on raw booked count guarantees you'll get gamed. **What happens if the business hands me a pipeline target above my team's capacity?** Add headcount or improve tooling and list quality — do not inflate the quota. A quota above real capacity doesn't create pipeline; it creates turnover and a flood of low-quality meetings from reps scrambling to hit an impossible bar. **Should a 6-person team have any team-based pay component?** Optionally a modest one — roughly 10–20% of variable tied to the team hitting its number — to encourage collaboration and knowledge-sharing. Keep the individual portion clearly dominant so accountability stays personal, or use non-monetary contests and spiffs to build culture without diluting individual comp. **How often should I revisit the plan?** Review it at least annually, and re-model the payout curve whenever your motion, list quality, deal size, or tooling changes materially. In 2027, blended human-plus-AI prospecting is shifting the SDR job toward judgment work — that shift can justify adjusting both the base and the metrics you pay on. **Do accelerators really matter for such a small team?** Yes — on a 6-person team your one or two overperformers carry an outsized share of the pipeline, and uncapped accelerators are how you keep them. Losing a top SDR to a competitor that pays overperformance is far more expensive than the incremental commission you'd have paid to retain them. **How do I handle unequal territories across six reps?** Rebalance the territories, or set per-rep quotas that reflect each patch's true potential. Never advertise a single OTE while quietly assigning unwinnable territories — on a small team the inequity is highly visible and will cost you your fairest-minded people first. ## Related on PULSE - [Comp-plan split fundamentals: base vs. variable](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-comp-split-basics) - [Activity vs. outcome metrics for SDR pay](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-sdr-metrics) - [Ramp periods and accelerator design](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-ramp-accelerators) - [Setting reachable sales quotas from capacity](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-quota-capacity) - [Rules of engagement for SDR-to-AE handoff](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-handoff-roe)
